# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

window.addEventListener( "message", function( e ) {
	if ( e.origin === "https://r-login.wordpress.com" ) {
		var data = {};
		try {
			data = JSON.parse( e.data );
		} catch( e ) {
			wpcom_remote_login_final_cleanup();
			return;
		}

		if ( data.msg === 'LOGIN' ) {
			// Clean up the login check iframe
			wpcom_remote_login_remove_dom_node_id( "wpcom_remote_login_key" );

			var id_regex = new RegExp( /^[0-9]+$/ );
			var token_regex = new RegExp( /^.*|.*|.*$/ );

				token_regex.test( data.token )
				&& id_regex.test( data.wpcomid )

			return;
		}

		// Safari ITP, storage access failed, remove the request

			// Check ITP iframe enable/disable knob

				return;

			try {
				var opendb = window.openDatabase( null, null, null, null );
			} catch( e ) {
				private_window = true;
			}

			if ( private_window ) {
				console.log( 'private window' );
				return;
			}

			var iframe = document.createElement( 'iframe' );
			iframe.id = 'wpcom_request_access_iframe';
			iframe.setAttribute( 'scrolling', 'no' );
			iframe.setAttribute( 'sandbox', 'allow-storage-access-by-user-activation allow-scripts allow-same-origin allow-top-navigation-by-user-activation' );
			iframe.src = 'https://r-login.wordpress.com/remote-login.php?wpcom_remote_login=request_access&origin=' + encodeURIComponent( data.origin ) + '&wpcomid=' + encodeURIComponent( data.wpcomid );

#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Homeland Infrastructure Foundation-Level Data (HIFLD) Open
Organization/publisher: Department of Homeland Security
Description: The public-facing portal for the HIFLD program, providing geospatial data and tools for planners, analysts, and others throughout the homeland security enterprise, supporting missions including law enforcement, border protection, emergency management, critical infrastructure protection, and national operations and data fusion centers.
URL: https://www.dhs.gov/gmo/hifld

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

I'll research the HIFLD Open dataset comprehensively. Let me start with several searches to verify the details and gather information from multiple angles.The page fetches returned mostly navigation boilerplate, but the search results gave me substantial content. Let me fill in a few remaining gaps on the program's origins, launch details, and research usage.# Research Report: Homeland Infrastructure Foundation-Level Data (HIFLD) Open

## ⚠️ Most Important Finding First

Your information was accurate **but is now out of date in one critical respect**: **HIFLD Open no longer exists as a live public portal.** DHS decommissioned it on **August 26, 2025**, and the portal and its hosted data services went completely offline after **September 16, 2025**. The URL you provided (https://www.dhs.gov/gmo/hifld) is still live, but it now describes the HIFLD *program* generally and points users to **HIFLD Secure**, a restricted-access system. The full archived data survives in several non-governmental repositories (details below). This status change is central to anything a preservationist, librarian, data scientist, or policy activist needs to know.

---

## 1. Verification of Your Submitted Information

| Field | Your claim | Verification |
|---|---|---|
| Title | Homeland Infrastructure Foundation-Level Data (HIFLD) Open | ✅ Accurate |
| Publisher | Department of Homeland Security | ✅ Accurate — specifically the DHS **Geospatial Management Office (GMO)**, within the DHS Office of the Chief Information Officer |
| Description | Public-facing portal for geospatial data supporting the homeland security enterprise | ⚠️ Accurate for 2016–August 2025; the portal is now **decommissioned** |
| URL | https://www.dhs.gov/gmo/hifld | ✅ Live, but now describes the program/HIFLD Secure rather than the open data portal. The former data portal URLs were `hifld-geoplatform.opendata.arcgis.com` (originally `hifld-dhs-gii.opendata.arcgis.com`), both now defunct |

---

## 2. What the Dataset Was

HIFLD Open was the public, unclassified half of the HIFLD program — a curated, centralized aggregation of **national foundation-level geospatial data on U.S. critical infrastructure**, drawn from dozens of federal agencies. At shutdown it contained roughly **500+ data layers** (the Data Rescue Project archived **415 layers**; counts vary by date and definition), covering all 50 states and U.S. territories.

**Thematic categories** (from the portal's own catalog): Agriculture, Borders, Boundaries, Chemicals, Commercial, Communications, Education, Emergency Services, Energy, Finance, Food Industry, Geonames, Government, Law Enforcement, Mail & Shipping, Mining, National Flood Hazard, Natural Hazards, Public Health, Public Venues, Transportation (Air, Ground, Water), and Water Supply. Concrete examples: power plants, electric substations and transmission lines, hospitals, nursing homes, schools, prisons and jails, airports, ports, bridges, water treatment plants, flood zones, and administrative boundaries.

**Content model:** A mix of (a) *re-hosted* public-domain datasets copied from source agencies and (b) *live pointers* to source agencies' dynamic web services. This is important for preservation: much of the underlying data was always published by originating agencies (USGS, DOE, Census, FEMA, FDA, etc.), and HIFLD's value was **aggregation, curation, standardization, and one-stop access** — not unique data creation.

**Formats and access:** Downloads in CSV, KML, Shapefile, and File Geodatabase; machine access via GeoJSON and ArcGIS GeoService/REST APIs; built on Esri's ArcGIS Open Data/Hub platform and integrated with Geoplatform.gov and Data.gov. **No account or login was ever required.**

---

## 3. Publisher and Governance

- **Managing office:** DHS Geospatial Management Office (GMO), which managed HIFLD "in partnership with representatives from agencies whose missions depend on reliable access to current, high-quality geospatial data," gathering use cases from across the homeland security enterprise (HSE) to prioritize layers, attributes, and coverage.
- **Interagency governance:** The **HIFLD Subcommittee** of the Federal Geographic Data Committee (FGDC), whose core membership included DHS (NPPD Office of Infrastructure Protection, now CISA), the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency (NGA), DOD's Office of the Assistant Secretary of Defense for Homeland Defense, and DOI/USGS. Per FGDC, this subcommittee was **retired in March 2026**, with DHS stating the GMO's HIFLD Program "meets or exceeds the original intent of the subcommittee."
- **Two-tier structure:** HIFLD Open (public) and **HIFLD Secure** (commercially licensed and FOUO/CUI data on the DHS Geospatial Information Infrastructure, or GII; access requires a GII account, an approved Data Use Agreement, and either a DHS PIV/CAC or a DHS-authorized Login.gov account with a federal sponsor). **HIFLD Secure continues to operate.**

## 4. Authority and Mandate

HIFLD grew out of the post-9/11 critical-infrastructure protection mandate rather than a single statute. Documented authorities include:

- **HSPD-7 (2003), ¶31:** directs the Secretary of Homeland Security to "develop a program… to geospatially map, image, analyze, and sort critical infrastructure and key resources." (Later superseded by PPD-21.)
- **Presidential Policy Directives PPD-8 (national preparedness) and PPD-21 (critical infrastructure security and resilience).**
- **OMB Circular A-16** (coordination of federal geospatial data, establishing the FGDC), **Executive Order 12906** (National Spatial Data Infrastructure), and the **E-Government Act of 2002** — cited in the HIFLD Subcommittee's FGDC charter, along with OMB Circulars A-119 and A-130.
- **Geospatial Data Act of 2018:** DHS, as a "covered agency," reported HIFLD activities in its annual FGDC self-assessments. Notably, DHS's FY2025 report describes the transition of all nationwide foundational geospatial infrastructure data from the public GeoPlatform into the secure GII environment as a "major change from previous fiscal years," occurring amid a "partial strategic pause" of GeoPlatform services.

## 5. History and Provenance

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| Post-9/11 | DHS initiative to catalog U.S. critical infrastructure begins |
| **Feb 2002** | HIFLD community/subcommittee established (per FGDC) to improve collection, sharing, and protection of homeland infrastructure geospatial information; a formal joint DOD/DHS/NGA/USGS working group charter dates to 2004 |
| 2002–2016 | Data distributed as the **Homeland Security Infrastructure Program (HSIP)**, sponsored and overseen by NGA. **HSIP Gold** mixed government and commercially licensed data, restricted to FOUO users and distributed **by postal-mailed DVDs**; **HSIP Freedom** was a limited attempt at wider state/local distribution |
| **Feb 24, 2016** | DHS GMO Director **David Alexander** announces **HIFLD Open** at the Esri FedGIS Conference, replacing HSIP Freedom with an ArcGIS Online open-data portal of ~274 datasets; the "HSIP" brand is retired. Esri reports the site was built in about a month |
| 2016 | Rapid uptake: over 9,000 users within months; ~320 public datasets |
| 2017–2018 | Security controversy: Arizona utility companies object to public energy layers (power plants, transmission lines, substations); ad-hoc review by DHS, DOE, ORNL, NGA — an early example of the aggregation-vs.-security debate |
| **Fall 2022** | NGA completes transfer of all HIFLD program authority and resources to a distinct program under the DHS GMO |
| **2025** | DHS announces discontinuation — initially by Sept 30, then moved up to **Aug 26, 2025**; the website and portal fully offline after **Sept 16, 2025**. DHS's stated justification: hosting the open portal was "no longer a priority for their mission." Some Open-only layers moved to HIFLD Secure (with new URLs); DHS published a **crosswalk** linking each layer to the originating agency's portal |
| **Dec 2025** | Data Rescue Project completes archiving of 415 layers in DataLumos |
| **Mar 2026** | FGDC formally retires the HIFLD Subcommittee |

## 6. Typical Users and Use Cases

- **Emergency management and first responders:** The National Alliance for Public Safety GIS (NAPSG) Foundation championed HIFLD Open for preparedness, response, and recovery. Data supported incident mapping for **Hurricanes Harvey, Irma, and Maria** and **California wildfires**.
- **Government mission partners:** FEMA, NORAD/NORTHCOM, the National Interagency Fire Center, U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, DOT; state, local, tribal, and territorial governments; law enforcement; border protection; and state/national **fusion centers**.
- **Researchers and data journalists:** e.g., the UCLA Law COVID-19 Behind Bars Data Project built its master U.S. prison/jail facility list on HIFLD layers; energy researchers used substation/transmission layers for grid and climate-resilience analysis; public health researchers used hospital and nursing-home layers.
- **Planners, businesses, and the public:** site suitability (e.g., alternative fueling stations, refrigerated warehouses), transit investment, community preparedness, and academic teaching (it was a staple of GIS curricula).

**Public benefits:** a single, no-login, machine-readable point of access to authoritative national infrastructure data that would otherwise require hunting across dozens of agency sites; standardized formats and metadata; and a common operating picture shared by federal, state, and local responders.

## 7. Licensing and Terms

HIFLD Open data was **public domain** (U.S. government works) with no account requirement; layers carried standard federal disclaimers regarding accuracy and currency. HIFLD Secure data, by contrast, is governed by Data Use Agreements, commercial licenses, and CUI/FOUO handling rules. Preservation copies carry their own wrappers: the SeerAI/Source Cooperative archive is released under CC BY 4.0, and DataLumos records carry a Public Domain Mark.

## 8. Preservation Status and Where the Data Lives Now

This is the most actionable section for preservationists and librarians:

1. **Data Rescue Project → DataLumos (ICPSR):** A full snapshot of **415 layers** captured before shutdown, completed December 2025, coordinated by Frank Donnelly (Head of GIS and Data Services, Brown University Library) with ~20 volunteers. Original formats preserved (GeoJSON, shapefile, geopackage, file geodatabase) plus metadata. Search "HIFLD Open" at datalumos.org; a **data index and the official DHS crosswalk** are archived as their own record (project 241367). **Bulk download** is available via Brown University Library's **Globus endpoint**.
2. **HIFLD Next (Public Environmental Data Partners):** hifld.publicenvirodata.org — a "versioned, living system" built on the Data Rescue snapshot, adding modern formats (GeoParquet, PMTiles), map/table viewers, and intent to track updates. Presented to the FGDC National Geospatial Advisory Committee in 2026.
3. **SeerAI archive on Source Cooperative:** source.coop/seerai/hifld — GeoParquet conversion of most layers, CC BY 4.0.
4. **Homeland Security Digital Library (HSDL)** at the Naval Postgraduate School's Center for Homeland Defense and Security (DHS-funded): preserved an aggregation of the open sources as a public resource (hsdl.org/hifld).
5. **Originating agencies:** The DHS crosswalk (Aug 2025) maps each layer to the source agency's own portal (USGS, DOE, FEMA, etc.), where many datasets continue to be updated — but the one-stop aggregation is gone.

**Key preservation caveat:** all archives are *static snapshots* as of August 2025. They will remain reasonably current for a couple of years, after which they serve primarily as a historical archive; for current data, users must consult source agencies individually.

## 9. Issues of Interest to Policy Activists

- **Open-data rollback:** HIFLD Open's shutdown is one of the most prominent cases in the 2025 wave of federal data removals. Critics note DHS offered no technical or budgetary rationale — only that public data "for community preparedness, resiliency, research, and more" was "no longer a priority." Per DHS's own FY2025 Geospatial Data Act report, even *public-domain* foundational data was moved into the access-controlled GII, raising questions about compliance with the spirit of the Geospatial Data Act and open-government commitments (OPEN Government Data Act).
- **Access inequity:** HIFLD Secure eligibility appears limited to users who "support a homeland security or homeland defense mission" with a federal sponsor — effectively excluding most researchers, journalists, local planners, and the public who previously relied on HIFLD Open.
- **The security-vs-openness tension is long-standing:** the 2017–18 Arizona utility dispute over energy infrastructure layers foreshadowed today's posture. Notably, the security research community has generally found that the aggregated public data posed marginal incremental risk, since the underlying data was already public at source agencies.
- **Governance dissolution:** The retirement of the FGDC HIFLD Subcommittee (2026) removes the interagency/volunteer forum that had coordinated this data community since 2002.

## 10. Key Sources

- DHS HIFLD program page: https://www.dhs.gov/gmo/hifld
- NAPSG Foundation transition notices and webinar: https://www.napsgfoundation.org/hifld_open/
- FGDC HIFLD Subcommittee page and 2014 charter: https://www.fgdc.gov/organization/working-groups-subcommittees/hifld
- NGA transfer announcement: https://www.nga.mil/news/NGA_transfers_Homeland_Security_Infrastructure_Pro.html
- 2016 launch coverage: NAPSG press release (Mar 3, 2016); Esri Insider; AFCEA Signal; FedScoop; geoMusings blog (excellent on HSIP Gold/Freedom history)
- Shutdown analysis: At These Coordinates (Aug 8 & Dec 27, 2025 posts, by Frank Donnelly): https://atcoordinates.info/2025/08/08/hifld-open-gis-portal-shuts-down-aug-26-2025/
- Data Rescue Project archive announcement: https://www.datarescueproject.org/hifld-data-saved/
- DataLumos index + DHS crosswalk: https://www.datalumos.org/datalumos/project/241367/version/V1/view
- HIFLD Next: https://hifld.publicenvirodata.org/about
- HSDL: https://www.hsdl.org/hifld/
- DHS FY2025 Geospatial Data Act report: https://www.fgdc.gov/gda/gda-ca-reports/FY25CoveredAgencyReports/FY25DHSGDAReport
- Independent metadata/shutdown report: https://urbanicity.space/assets/docs/HIFLD_Shutdown_Metadata_Report.pdf

**Bottom line:** Your cataloging metadata correctly identifies the title and publisher, but any current record should be updated to reflect that HIFLD Open was decommissioned in August 2025, that the surviving access points are the DataLumos archive (canonical snapshot), HIFLD Next (living derivative), and source-agency portals (via the DHS crosswalk), and that the HIFLD program itself continues only in restricted form as HIFLD Secure.

# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>

Policy: <level>

I'll do additional research on the current agency context — DHS staffing, leadership, and policy — to inform the rubric categories.# Risk Assessment: Homeland Infrastructure Foundation-Level Data (HIFLD) Open

**Critical framing note:** This assessment differs from most in one decisive way — the risk has already materialized. DHS **terminated HIFLD Open on August 26, 2025**, and the portal and its hosted services went fully offline after **September 16, 2025**. DHS's stated rationale was that hosting the open portal was "no longer a priority for their mission." The rubric's "Gone" levels therefore describe present reality for several categories. I also assess residual risk to what remains (HIFLD Secure, source-agency data, and the unofficial archives), since those are the only access paths left.

---

## Historical Data Availability

**Evidence by level:**
- **Gone:** The HIFLD Open portal — the primary location — was decommissioned; its URLs (`hifld-geoplatform.opendata.arcgis.com`) are defunct. All ~415–500+ public layers were removed from DHS hosting. DHS re-hosts nothing publicly; it published only a crosswalk pointing to source agencies. (NAPSG, Aug 2025; At These Coordinates, Aug 8 & Dec 27, 2025; DHS HIFLD page)
- **High Risk:** Some layers removed — superseded, since *all* were removed.
- **Moderate Risk:** Some data elements removed — superseded.
- **No Known Issue:** Not applicable to the primary location. *Mitigating factor:* the full final snapshot (415 layers, original formats + metadata) was captured before shutdown by the Data Rescue Project and is archived in DataLumos (ICPSR), with derivatives at HIFLD Next, HSDL, and Source Cooperative. Much of the underlying data also still lives at originating agencies. However, these are third-party archives, not the primary location, and the underlying data at source agencies was never uniformly mirrored by HIFLD.

**Assessment: Gone.** The entire historical public corpus was removed from its primary location in August 2025. Accurate copies survive only because of pre-shutdown community archiving; there is no government-hosted public historical record.

## Future Data Availability

**Evidence by level:**
- **Gone:** DHS explicitly announced discontinuation of HIFLD Open (initially by Sept 30, then accelerated to Aug 26, 2025). There is no ICR, no publication schedule, and no successor federal public service. HIFLD Open "is no longer available on geoplatform.gov" (NAPSG transition webinar, Sept 2025).
- **High/Moderate Risk:** Missed deadlines, skipped cycles, expired ICR — superseded by outright termination.
- **No Known Issue:** Applies only to **HIFLD Secure**, which continues (DHS held a "2026 HIFLD User Forum" describing FY25–26 deprecations, updates, and additions to HIFLD Shared/Secure) — but Secure requires a GII account, an approved Data Use Agreement, and a federal sponsor, excluding the public, most researchers, and journalists.

**Assessment: Gone.** Public data publication has been terminated. For nongovernmental users, future data availability now depends on a volunteer-run successor (HIFLD Next, launched March 2026 by Public Environmental Data Partners) and piecemeal agency portals.

## Data Quality

**Evidence by level:**
- **Gone:** Publication terminated; no federal updates to the open corpus are occurring. All archives are static snapshots as of August 2025 and will degrade in currency (the Data Rescue Project itself cautions snapshots remain "reasonably current" for only a couple of years).
- **High Risk:** DHS's FY2025 Geospatial Data Act report documents FY25–26 **deprecations** of layers even within HIFLD Secure, and the 2026 HIFLD User Forum openly lists deprecations alongside updates. Live pointers in archived layers now break as source URLs change (an independent metadata report found the archived URLs already "aging").
- **Moderate Risk:** DHS OIG (OIG-25-34, Aug 2025) found DHS components understaffed for geospatial work — needing **42 FTEs across 7 components** to meet GDA responsibilities — an emerging risk to the quality of the underlying source data that fed HIFLD.
- **No Known Issue:** HIFLD Next is adding modern formats, versioning, and updated layers (e.g., an updated hospitals layer), but this is a grassroots effort without federal resourcing.

**Assessment: Gone** for the federal dataset. **(High Risk** for the de facto successor ecosystem, which depends on volunteer maintenance and decaying source links.)

## Statutory Context

**Evidence by level:**
- **High Risk:** HIFLD's authority rests on presidential directives — **HSPD-7 (2003) ¶31** ("geospatially map, image, analyze, and sort critical infrastructure") and **PPD-21** — plus OMB Circular A-16 and the Geospatial Data Act of 2018 (which governs geospatial *coordination and metadata*, not public publication of this aggregation). Crucially, **nothing in statute requires a public-facing open data service**; HIFLD Open was a discretionary program interpretation. The March 13, 2025 DHS directives and **E.O. 14239** ("Achieving Efficiency Through State and Local Preparedness") actively reorient critical infrastructure risk management toward states, and the Administration terminated the prior public-private coordination framework (CRS R48878). Alternative collections exist in fragments at source agencies, but no substitute one-stop aggregation.
- **Moderate Risk:** The broader HIFLD program is required for implementation of federal homeland security programs (fusion centers, FEMA, NORTHCOM) — true, but this sustains only HIFLD *Secure*, not public access.
- **No Known Issue:** Not applicable — no statute explicitly names HIFLD Open or mandates public dissemination.

**Assessment: High Risk** (rubric marks Gone as N/A here). The statutory basis is vague/directive-based with respect to *public* access, substitutes exist in theory, and the Administration's policy framework actively deprioritizes centralized federal provision. This vagueness is precisely what enabled termination without legal barrier.

## Staffing and Funding

**Evidence by level:**
- **Gone:** No evidence the GMO itself was eliminated — it still runs HIFLD Secure and hosted the 2026 HIFLD User Forum. But the staff/contractor capacity supporting the *Open* portal is effectively gone with the program.
- **High Risk:** Substantial supporting evidence: (a) Secretary Noem directed cuts of **~50% of the DHS Management Directorate** (~3,900 FTE), which houses the CIO's office and thus GMO (Federal News Network, Apr 2025); (b) **CISA lost ~33% of staff** (3,400 → 2,500, FY24–25) and the FY26 budget request would cut ~1,000 more; (c) **FEMA lost ~2,000+ staff (~one-third of permanent workforce)** and 24 senior executives; (d) DHS I&A targeted to shrink from ~1,000 toward 500; (e) DHS OIG had already flagged geospatial staffing gaps (42 FTEs needed; GMO had only **10 federal FTEs** as of late 2024); (f) **leadership turnover**: DHS has a new Secretary (Markwayne Mullin, per the current dhs.gov banner, replacing Noem), and the CX directorate head departed amid the cuts. Cuts hit DHS HQ/OCIO-adjacent units (AI Corps, CX) specifically as "non-mission critical" — the same logic DHS applied to HIFLD Open.
- **Moderate Risk:** GAO shows DHS department-wide headcount declined only ~1–3% (law enforcement exempt) — but this masks the concentration of losses in exactly the management/geospatial/data functions relevant here.
- **No Known Issue:** Not applicable.

**Assessment: High Risk.** The offices surrounding HIFLD (Management Directorate/OCIO, CISA, FEMA) have lost or are targeted for losses far exceeding the 40%/20% thresholds, leadership has turned over, and the 10-person GMO was already flagged by the OIG as under-resourced before the cuts. (For the Open program specifically, the truthful characterization is "Gone.")

## Policy

**Evidence by level:**
- **Gone:** Publication was terminated in direct accordance with Administration priorities — DHS's only stated reason was mission reprioritization, and it occurred alongside E.O. 14239, the March 13, 2025 DHS directives devolving critical infrastructure functions to states, and the elimination of the prior critical-infrastructure partnership framework (CRS R48878).
- **High Risk:** "Negative policy note on site" — the DHS HIFLD page now functions as exactly that, redirecting users to the gated HIFLD Secure. Even *public-domain* foundational layers were moved behind access controls, per DHS's own FY25 GDA report. The FGDC HIFLD Subcommittee — the interagency governance body since 2002 — was **retired in March 2026**.
- **Moderate Risk:** CRS reports a "new framework with unspecified reforms… in active consideration as of early 2026," and the National Resilience Strategy required by E.O. 14239 remains unreleased — pending changes with unclear implications for public data.
- **No Known Issue:** Clearly not applicable.

**Assessment: Gone.** The termination was itself a policy action of the current Administration, and no announced policy contemplates restoration of public access.

## Summary

| Category | Level |
|---|---|
| Historical Data Availability | **Gone** |
| Future Data Availability | **Gone** |
| Data Quality | **Gone** (High Risk for volunteer-maintained successors) |
| Statutory Context | **High Risk** (Gone = N/A per rubric; vague directive-based authority, no mandate for public access) |
| Staffing and Funding | **High Risk** (functionally Gone for the Open program; >30–50% cuts in surrounding offices, leadership turnover, pre-existing understaffing per DHS OIG) |
| Policy | **Gone** |

**Bottom line:** HIFLD Open is not "at risk" — it is a realized loss, terminated by DHS in August 2025 as an explicit act of administrative reprioritization, enabled by weak statutory footing and carried out amid deep staffing cuts to DHS's data and geospatial functions. The data survives only through pre-shutdown rescue archiving (DataLumos/ICPSR — canonical snapshot), a volunteer successor (HIFLD Next), a DHS-funded library aggregation (HSDL), and fragmented source-agency portals (via the DHS crosswalk). None of these is being updated by DHS for public users; the only live federal version, HIFLD Secure, is closed to the public. Preservation efforts should treat the August 2025 snapshot as the final federal edition and prioritize monitoring the sustainability of HIFLD Next and the continued availability of source-agency layers.
